memory_candidates.content: A rank-based 'monotonic-max' status clamp (comparing lifecycle ranks to decide whether a forced status write would regress) does NOT protect a status that is deliberately left UNRANKED/omitted from the rank table -- the clamp's own 'unranked means no regression, write proceeds' rule lets an ordinary forced write through unguarded. If a new status must be STICKY (survive an otherwise-forced write unconditionally, e.g. a human-set pause that must outlast a one-off forcing-flag override), it needs a DEDICATED guard keyed on the CURRENT status value itself (e.g. 'if current status is X, downgrade every write except the X-set/X-lift operations to a status-field no-op'), not an extension of the rank table. Verify this by tracing the exact live call chain (e.g. skill_preflight_update -> the status-writer script) end-to-end against a scratch fixture, not just the dispatch-planning layer in isolation -- the planning layer (e.g. a dry-run plan builder) can correctly show the write being ADMITTED while a separate layer (the actual status writer) is what must prevent the status FIELD from changing.

To regression-test a bash snippet embedded in a markdown command file (e.g. commands/*.md, which is documentation executed by an agent at runtime, not a sourced script), extract the exact snippet with awk anchored on distinctive start/end lines directly from the source-store file, verify the extraction actually contains the expected new code (grep for a marker string) before trusting it, then `eval` it inside a subshell with the needed input variables pre-set and cwd pointed at a synthetic fixture directory. This is the only way to exercise such logic in an automated test without invoking the full agent/command dispatch machinery, and catches drift between the documented STAGE 0-style bash and what a test suite assumes it does.
